planting.note: Broadcast seed onto bare, open sand after the last frost; this species needs exposed mineral soil and will not establish through litter or dense thatch.

directions: Seaside threeawn is a wiry, clump-forming bunchgrass of open sandplain grasslands and blowouts on Cape Cod, the Elizabeth Islands, and outer Long Island, where it colonizes bare, nutrient-poor sand alongside poverty oatgrass and golden heather. Its large, strongly contorted awns twist and untwist with changing humidity, literally screwing the seed into loose sand for self-planting. Grow it in full sun on droughty, well-drained sand with no irrigation or fertility once established; it declines quickly if shaded out by taller grasses or woody encroachment, so periodic mowing or burning is needed to keep habitat open. It is state-rare across much of New England, so source seed only from regional ecotype collections.
sources: Massachusetts Natural Heritage & Endangered Species Program sandplain grassland fact sheets

planting.note: Fall-sow onto open sand so winter freeze-thaw cycles help break seed dormancy; cold stratification improves spring emergence.

directions: Beach pinweed is a low, wiry subshrub with tiny scale-like leaves and inconspicuous flowers that forms loose mats among the dwarf ericaceous shrubs of coastal heathland and sandplain grassland from Cape Cod to eastern Long Island. It tolerates salt spray, sand burial, and extreme drought, flowering in a short burst of small reddish-brown blossoms in late summer that are easy to overlook against the sand. Site it in full sun on coarse, infertile, excessively drained sand; it has no tolerance for rich soil, mulch, or competition from taller vegetation. Because it is slow from seed and rarely offered outside regional conservation nurseries, division of small rooted mats is the more reliable propagation route for gardeners.
sources: New England Wild Flower Society (Native Plant Trust) rare plant program notes

planting.note: Sow fresh seed on open sand in autumn; seed needs an overwinter chill and bare mineral soil contact to germinate well.

directions: Racemed milkwort is a short-lived biennial-to-perennial wildflower of dry, sandy barrens and sandplain grasslands, sending up basal rosettes one year and spikes of pink-purple (and often a second crop of self-pollinating cleistogamous white) flowers close to the ground the next. It is a classic indicator of open, disturbed sand in the company of poverty oatgrass, little bluestem, and frostweed, and it fades quickly once leaf litter or woody shrubs shade the ground. Grow in full sun on lean, acidic, excessively drained sand with no supplemental fertility; periodic fire or mowing that resets bare patches keeps a population self-sustaining. It reseeds readily where open sand persists but does not compete in ordinary garden beds.
sources: Massachusetts Natural Heritage & Endangered Species Program

planting.note: Surface-sow onto bare sand in early spring; seed is tiny and needs light plus mineral soil contact, not burial.

directions: Sand wormwood (ssp. caudata, the coastal New England race) is a finely cut, silvery, aromatic biennial-to-short-lived-perennial that threads through open sandplain grassland and dune-edge heathland from Cape Cod to eastern Long Island. Its single or sparsely branched flowering stem bears small nodding greenish heads in late summer, far less showy than its airy, dissected foliage. It needs full sun and loose, infertile, well-drained sand, declining wherever thatch, shade, or nutrient enrichment builds up, so it is best paired with other bare-sand specialists like beach pinweed and poverty grass. It is rare across much of its New England range, so gardeners should seek regional ecotype seed rather than western or Great Plains sources of the species.

planting.note: Transplant container stock in fall onto open sand; if growing from seed, cold-stratify pits over winter before spring sowing, as germination is slow and uneven.

directions: Appalachian sand cherry is a small, erect, colony-forming shrub of sandplain grasslands and barrens, distinguished from the low, mat-forming Prunus pumila of dunes by its taller upright habit and finely pubescent twigs. White spring flowers along the bare stems give way to small dark cherries that ripen in a landscape otherwise dominated by bunchgrasses and dwarf heaths, providing an important early-season nectar and fruit source for sandplain wildlife. It demands full sun and coarse, acidic, excessively drained sand, and resents both shade and rich garden soil. Periodic disturbance such as fire or mowing keeps competing woody growth down and maintains the open structure this species depends on.

planting.note: Sow onto open sand in spring after frost danger passes; seed benefits from brief heat or smoke exposure mimicking the fire regime that resets its sandplain habitat.

directions: Bushy frostweed is a dwarf, woody-based subshrub endemic to the sandplain grasslands and coastal heathlands of southeastern New England and eastern Long Island, growing alongside golden heather and poverty oatgrass on fire- and mowing-maintained outwash plains. Small yellow five-petaled flowers open only in strong morning sun and drop by midday, followed later by inconspicuous self-pollinated flowers lower on the stem, a frostweed-genus trait. It requires full sun and lean, acidic, excessively drained sand, declining rapidly if shrub or tree cover closes in, which is why its last strongholds depend on prescribed fire or mowing regimes. It is globally rare and known from only a handful of occurrences, so seed or divisions should come only from regional conservation or native-plant-society propagation programs rather than wild collection.
sources: Massachusetts Natural Heritage & Endangered Species Program
